annotation_description: With an aggressive red deck featuring two Hired Claws, a Stadium Headliner, Might of the Meek, and two Leyline of Resonance (one already starting on the battlefield for free), this is a classic aggro hand that benefits significantly from going first. Playing first means deploying Hired Claw on turn 1 and attacking on turn 2 before the opponent has established any defense. The tempo advantage of going first with a low-curve aggro deck is well-established.

message: Select a card (1 more) to put on the bottom of your library
annotation_description: Bottomed Might of the Meek, which is a cantrip pump spell that both triggers Slickshot Show-Off's +2/+0 ability AND replaces itself, making it one of the best cards in this hand. Stadium Headliner is a 1/1 that doesn't synergize with the Slickshot gameplan and doesn't trigger the +2/+0 ability.

Stadium Headliner is a 1/1 that creates attacking tokens with Mobilize 1, and can sacrifice itself to deal damage equal to creatures controlled. While it's only a 1/1, it can snowball value by creating tokens each attack, and its sacrifice ability could become relevant. Get Lost would cleanly remove it at the cost of giving opponent two Map tokens. However, the opponent only has one Mountain and the Headliner is a low-impact threat at this stage. The Map tokens could help the opponent find lands and improve card quality. With two copies of No More Lies in hand, the player may prefer to hold up countermagic for more impactful threats. Not using Get Lost here is defensible but worth considering since the Headliner's Mobilize triggers add up and the sacrifice ability scales with creature count.

Playing Fire Nation Palace before combat with an aggressive deck holding combat tricks (Full Bore, Turn Inside Out, Dreadmaw's Ire) and a Stadium Headliner ready to attack. While Fire Nation Palace enters untapped (since a basic Mountain is controlled), the player should consider whether attacking first with Stadium Headliner before playing the land would be better to avoid giving information. More importantly, the player could consider plotting Slickshot Show-Off this turn (costs 1R, which they have with Mountain + Fire Nation Palace), but that's actually fine since they need to play the land first to have the mana. The land play itself is reasonable, but there's a question of whether Mountain would have been better to keep open more flexible mana options and save Fire Nation Palace for later when its firebending ability becomes relevant. However, Fire Nation Palace entering untapped and providing red mana is functionally similar to Mountain here, and plotting Slickshot Show-Off is enabled either way.

Plotting Slickshot Show-Off on turn 2 uses both mana lands but delays the creature by a turn. Since Slickshot has haste naturally, plotting it doesn't gain the haste benefit (it already has it). The main advantage of plotting is casting it for free on a later turn to save mana for pump spells. However, with Stadium Headliner already on board ready to attack, the player could have held the Slickshot and played the Mountain from hand first (ensuring the land drop), then attacked with Stadium Headliner this turn. By plotting now, they tap out and can't use Fire Nation Palace's firebending ability or hold up any combat tricks. More importantly, they should play their Mountain land first before spending mana - though in this case plotting does use exactly 2 mana (1R) and they have Mountain + Fire Nation Palace available. The sequencing of plotting before playing the Mountain land drop is the real issue - they should play Mountain first to have more options, then decide whether to plot or just cast Slickshot next turn with pump spell mana available.

Using Get Lost on Stadium Headliner (a 4/3 creature) on turn 3 when the opponent is tapped out gives them two Map tokens, which provide card selection advantage. With two copies of No More Lies in hand and only 2 lands (both Floodfarm Verge), the player could instead hold up No More Lies next turn to counter the opponent's next threat while developing their mana. Stadium Headliner is a reasonable threat to remove, but spending premium removal this early when holding counterspells and the opponent is tapped out (meaning they can't pressure immediately next turn without casting something new) is debatable. The Map tokens given are real value for an aggressive red deck.

Casting Emberheart Challenger before combat is suboptimal when holding three combat tricks (Dreadmaw's Ire, Full Bore, Turn Inside Out). Slickshot Show-Off is already on the battlefield with flying and haste. By casting a creature before combat, the player misses the opportunity to pump Slickshot with noncreature spells during combat for maximum damage. Additionally, casting Emberheart Challenger pre-combat telegraphs the threat and doesn't trigger Slickshot's pump ability (since it's a creature spell). The opponent has only 2 tapped lands, so there's no interaction to worry about. The better line is to attack with Slickshot first, then use combat tricks to pump it, and cast Emberheart Challenger post-combat (it has haste so it could attack, but playing tricks on Slickshot's attack is likely higher damage output).

Chose Dreadmaw's Ire over Full Bore or Turn Inside Out as the combat trick. With no blockers and opponent's lands tapped, Dreadmaw's Ire's trample and artifact destruction are irrelevant. Full Bore or Turn Inside Out on Emberheart Challenger would deal 9 total damage (vs 8 with Dreadmaw's Ire) while also triggering Emberheart's Valiant ability for a free card.

annotation_description: Slickshot Show-Off is arguably the more dangerous threat here. It has flying (harder to block), haste, and gets +2/+0 per noncreature spell cast, meaning it can deal massive burst damage in a single turn. Emberheart Challenger is a 2/2 with haste and prowess (+1/+1 per noncreature spell), which is less explosive. The opponent already used Dreadmaw's Ire from the graveyard, suggesting they're building around combat tricks with Slickshot. At 10 life, Grok4F Valley is particularly vulnerable to Slickshot's flying burst damage since they have no creatures to block flyers. Slickshot with just two pump spells represents 7+ damage in the air that can't be blocked.

Player has lethal damage available this turn with Slickshot Show-Off (flying) + Turn Inside Out + Full Bore = 11 power flying against opponent at 10 life with no blockers and all lands tapped. Activating a Map token first spends 1 of 3 available mana unnecessarily, leaving exactly 2 mana for the pump spells but adding risk and gaining nothing meaningful.

Missed lethal. Opponent is at 10 life with no untapped lands. Slickshot Show-Off has flying and the opponent has no flyers. By going to combat and casting both Full Bore (R) and Turn Inside Out (R) on the attacking Slickshot, it would be: 1 base + 4 from two prowess triggers + 3 from Full Bore + 3 from Turn Inside Out = 11 flying damage, which is lethal against 10 life. Activating the Map token spends one of the two available mana, making it impossible to cast both pump spells.

Spending the last untapped mana on a Map token explore instead of saving it for a devastating combat trick. Opponent is at 10 life with no creatures and tapped out. Full Bore during combat would make Slickshot a 6/4 flyer (base 1/2 + 2/0 Slickshot trigger + 3/2 Full Bore = 6/4), dealing 6 damage and leaving opponent at 4. Instead, exploring gives at best a +1/+1 counter with no mana left for tricks.

Cast Emberheart Challenger pre-combat spending 2 of 3 available mana, reducing the ability to cast both pump spells on Slickshot Show-Off during combat. With Slickshot's flying and the opponent at 6 life with no creatures, attacking and casting both Turn Inside Out (R) and Full Bore (R) would deal 11 flying damage for massive overkill lethal. After casting Emberheart Challenger (1R), only 1 mana remains, allowing only one pump spell for exactly 6 damage - still lethal but with zero margin for error.

Sonnet Gramps missed lethal by not casting Full Bore during combat. With both Slickshot Show-Off and Emberheart Challenger attacking into an empty board against an opponent at 6 life, casting Full Bore on either creature would deal 9 damage (target gets +3 power, both prowess creatures get +1/+1). Even if the opponent counters Full Bore with No More Lies, both prowess triggers still resolve, making the attackers 3/3 each for exactly 6 lethal damage. The reasoning incorrectly states the opponent is already dead at -6 life.
